title: Labyrinth Seal

introduction.definition: A labyrinth seal is a non-contacting seal used on compressors, turbines and bearing housings. A row of knife-edge teeth runs with a small clearance to the shaft; leaking gas is throttled at each tooth and loses its energy in the cavity after it, so pressure drops in steps and leakage stays small without any rubbing.
applications: Interstage and shaft-end seals of centrifugal compressors and steam turbines
Bearing-housing isolators and oil seals on pumps, fans and gearboxes
key_points: Non-contacting → no wear in normal running
Leakage falls with more teeth and smaller clearance
Buffer / eductor port at a middle cavity
introduction.summary: A labyrinth seal is a non-contacting shaft seal: a series of knife-edge teeth with tiny clearances throttles the gas leaking along the shaft step by step, keeping leakage low without any rubbing contact.

pressure.title: Pressure drops step by step
pressure.description: A labyrinth seal is a non-contacting seal: gas leaking along the shaft is forced through a series of tiny clearances at the knife-edge teeth. At each tooth it accelerates and loses pressure; in the cavity after it the jet's kinetic energy is dissipated as turbulence instead of being recovered. Pressure therefore falls in steps from the high-pressure side to the low-pressure side. Leakage falls with more teeth and smaller clearance, but never reaches zero; a buffer-gas or eductor port at a middle cavity can stop process gas escaping.

video_tutorials.title: Labyrinth Seal — Introduction

script.narration: This module introduces the Labyrinth Seal.
A labyrinth seal is a non-contacting seal used on compressors, turbines and bearing housings.

A row of knife-edge teeth runs with a small clearance to the shaft; leaking gas is throttled at each tooth and loses its energy in the cavity after it, so pressure drops in steps and leakage stays small without any rubbing.
Typical applications include interstage and shaft-end seals of centrifugal compressors and steam turbines; bearing-housing isolators and oil seals on pumps, fans and gearboxes.
The cutaway reveals the internal construction: Casing / Diaphragm holding the Seal, Rotor Shaft (turning; tooth tips run with small radial clearance).

script.narration: How the Labyrinth Seal works.
High-pressure gas reaches the first tooth.
It accelerates through the tiny clearance and loses pressure.
Its kinetic energy is dissipated as turbulence in the cavity.
The process repeats at every tooth until the low-pressure side.
The flow overlay traces the liquid from suction to discharge.
A labyrinth seal is a non-contacting seal: gas leaking along the shaft is forced through a series of tiny clearances at the knife-edge teeth.

video_tutorials.title: Labyrinth Seal — Maintenance

script.narration: Maintenance essentials for the Labyrinth Seal.
Trend leakage / buffer flow and bearing temperatures.
Inspect for rub marks during outages.
Replace damaged labyrinths; restore clearance.
Watch for excess leakage: high buffer flow, efficiency loss. Common cause: teeth rubbed (vibration, thermal bow).
Watch for oil leak at bearing labyrinth: oil at the shaft. Common cause: drain blocked, pressurised housing.
Record every inspection so trends — vibration, temperature, leakage and performance — can be compared over time.
